summary: After every preposition the Arabic noun is in the genitive (الْجَرّ): -i with the article (فِي الْبَيْتِ), -in without it (فِي بَيْتٍ). Arabic does not change the case for “where?”, “where to?” and “where from?” as German does (in der / in die Schule): the preposition alone shows the direction — فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ, إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, مِنَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ, all genitive. The genitive also marks the second noun of a construct: مَكْتَبُ الْبَرِيدِ (the office of the post), غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ. Some nouns show it differently: diptotes take -a when indefinite (فِي مَدَارِسَ), sound masculine plurals and duals end in -īna / -ayni (مَعَ الْمُهَنْدِسِينَ, مَعَ طَبِيبَيْنِ), feminine plurals in -āti(n), and defective nouns do not change at all (فِي الْمَقْهَى, فِي الْمُسْتَشْفَى, مَعَ مُحَامٍ, فِي الْقُرَى). With this the three cases are complete: nominative for the subject (lesson 4), accusative for the object (lesson 7), genitive after prepositions.

blocks.caption: The three Arabic cases, now complete.

blocks.title: The construct: the second noun is genitive.
blocks.text: مَكْتَبُ الْبَرِيدِ (the post office), غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ (the bedroom): the second noun is genitive; the first has no article and no tanwīn and takes the case of its place — فِي مَكْتَبِ الْبَرِيدِ, إِلَى غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ.

blocks.title: Diptotes: -a for the genitive.
blocks.text: Without the article a diptote has no tanwīn and takes -a in the genitive: فِي مَدَارِسَ, مِنْ شَوَارِعَ, مَعَ أَطِبَّاءَ. With the article it is normal again: فِي الْمَدَارِسِ.

blocks.title: Place words are nouns too.
blocks.text: تَحْتَ, أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ, دَاخِلَ, خَارِجَ end in -a because they are nouns in the accusative (“the place below”, “the front” …); the noun after them is genitive: تَحْتَ الطَّاوِلَةِ, أَمَامَ الْبَيْتِ (lesson 12).

items: plural, dual, defective? → its own ending

blocks.text: In speech and in the pause at the end of a sentence the short endings disappear (fi l-bēt), as with the other cases; the long endings -īna, -ayni are always said. This course writes every ending.

askYourself: Is there a preposition (فِي، إِلَى، مِنْ، عِنْدَ، مَعَ، بِـ، لِـ، عَنْ، بِدُونِ، عَلَى، تَحْتَ …) right before the noun? → genitive.
Does the noun have al- or a possessive ending? → -i; no al-? → -in.
Is it a diptote (مَدَارِسُ, شَوَارِعُ, مَطَاعِمُ, أَطِبَّاءُ)? → without al- the genitive is -a, with no tanwīn.
Is it a sound plural or a dual? → -īna, -āti(n), -ayni.
Is it defective (مَقْهًى, مُسْتَشْفًى, مُحَامٍ, قُرًى)? → no visible change.
Is it the second noun of a construct? → genitive; the first noun takes the case of its own place.
Where, where to, where from? → change the preposition, not the case.

traps: *فِي الْبَيْتُ → فِي الْبَيْتِ: never a nominative after a preposition.
*فِي الْبَيْتٍ: the article and tanwīn never go together.
*إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةَ: there is no accusative of direction as in German (in die Schule) — إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ.
Sound plurals: مَعَ الْمُهَنْدِسِينَ, not *مَعَ الْمُهَنْدِسُونَ.
In a construct only the second noun has al-: فِي مَكْتَبِ الْبَرِيدِ, not *فِي الْمَكْتَبِ الْبَرِيدِ.

quiz.why: After a preposition: genitive, -i with the article.
Indefinite genitive: -in (tanwīn), and never together with al-.
Arabic shows the direction with the preposition (إِلَى), not with the case as German does (in die Schule).
مَدَارِسُ is a diptote: no tanwīn, and -a in the indefinite genitive.
The sound masculine plural has -īna in the genitive (and accusative).
A defective noun in -ā (ى) shows no case ending.
A construct: the first word takes the genitive of its place without al-, the second word has al- and is genitive.

seeAlso.note:
German chooses the case after in, an, auf …:
- dative for “where?” — in der Schule;
- accusative for “where to?” — in die Schule.

Arabic always uses the genitive and changes the preposition (فِي / إِلَى).

Modern Hebrew has no cases — the noun never changes; only the preposition does:
→ בְּבֵית סֵפֶר, לְבֵית סֵפֶר

Arabic keeps the old Semitic genitive -i.

Chinese has no cases at all — the place word stays the same:
→ 在学校 (at school), 去学校 (to school)
The three case endings were introduced in lesson 4 (nominative) and lesson 7 (accusative); the genitive completes them.

notes.text: Greek prepositions also take a case (σε / από + accusative); Arabic always takes the genitive, whatever the preposition.
Russian chooses the case by preposition and meaning (в школе / в школу, из школы); Arabic has one case after every preposition: the genitive.
Spanish nouns never change after a preposition; Arabic nouns take the genitive -i / -in: فِي الْبَيْتِ.
English changes only pronouns after a preposition (with me); Arabic changes every noun: فِي الْبَيْتِ, مَعَ أَبِيكَ.

Hindi puts a noun into its oblique form before every postposition:
→ लड़का → लड़के से

Arabic puts it into the genitive after every preposition — **one form for all, in both**.

Persian nouns do not change after prepositions.

The Arabic construct is the counterpart of the Persian ezafe, but **it marks the second noun with the genitive** instead of linking with -e:
→ خانهٔ پدر — بَيْتُ الْأَبِ (the father’s house)
Marathi also uses an oblique stem before endings and postpositions; Arabic uses one genitive after every preposition.
Turkish has separate cases for place, direction and source (-de, -e, -den); Arabic has one genitive and lets the preposition say where.
Japanese particles never change the noun; Arabic prepositions put it into the genitive (-i / -in).
Finnish uses six local cases for in / into / out of and on / onto / off; Arabic has one genitive and lets the preposition carry the meaning.
Hungarian has many local cases (házban, házba, házból …); Arabic uses a preposition + the genitive.
Swahili nouns do not change after prepositions (kwa, na); Arabic nouns take the genitive.
Vietnamese nouns never change; Arabic nouns take the genitive after every preposition.
Inuktitut says in / to / from with case endings (-mi, -mut, -mit); Arabic with a preposition + the genitive.

French nouns never change after a preposition (dans la maison, de la maison).

Arabic nouns take **the genitive -i / -in after every preposition**:
→ فِي الْبَيْتِ, مِنْ بَيْتٍ

German chooses the case by preposition and by “where?” / “where to?”:
→ in der Schule / in die Schule

Arabic has **one case after every preposition, the genitive**, and lets the preposition say the direction:
→ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ, إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ

Chinese nouns stay the same after 在, 从 and 到; Arabic nouns change their ending after a preposition:
→ فِي الْبَيْتِ, مِنَ الْبَيْتِ, إِلَى الْبَيْتِ

Italian nouns never change after a preposition (in casa, da casa).

Arabic nouns take **the genitive -i / -in after every preposition**:
→ فِي الْبَيْتِ, فِي بَيْتٍ

Portuguese nouns never change after a preposition (na escola, da escola).

Arabic nouns take **the genitive -i / -in after every preposition**:
→ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ, مِنَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ
If your language says in / to / from with case suffixes, Arabic says it with a preposition before the noun — فِي, إِلَى, مِنْ — and puts the noun into **one case, the genitive**.

If your nouns never change, remember one rule: **after any preposition the noun ends in -i** (with the article) or -in (without).
→ فِي الْبَيْتِ, فِي بَيْتٍ
If your language marks in / to / from with endings on the place word, Arabic uses separate prepositions before the noun, which then takes the genitive.

If your language is Semitic, prepositions before the noun are familiar (بِـ, لِـ, مِنْ).

New is that the noun after them takes **a genitive ending, -i**.
